analytic.title: Energy Aware Real Time Scheduling Algorithm for Mixed Task Set

div.p: Energy consumption is one of the major limiting factors of battery operated real-time systems. Optimizing energy consumption without affecting performance and schedulability is the major topic to be researched. In this paper, an energy aware real time scheduling algorithm is proposed for a system with mixed task set consisting of both periodic and aperiodic tasks. Dynamic energy reduction techniques like Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) is used for energy optimization without affecting the responsiveness of aperiodic tasks. Performance of the proposed algorithm is compared with non-DVS algorithm. Experimental evaluation reveals that the proposed algorithm saves 54.44% of energy in comparison with non-DVS algorithms. It achieves this with no degradation in responsiveness of the aperiodic tasks.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Energy consumption is one of the major challenges to be addressed in battery operated high performance real-time systems. There exists various energy optimization techniques implemented at hardware-level, operating system level, instruction set architecture level and compiler level [1]. One of the popular techniques to optimize energy consumption at operating system level is DVFS [1,2,3] in scheduling. In this technique, supply voltage and clock frequency are dynamically adjusted based on the available slack time to reduce the energy consumption while scheduling. Some of the widely used dynamic slack estimation methods for periodic task set [3] are stretching to Next Arrival Time (NTA), utilization updating and priority based slack stealing . Most of the algorithms are developed based on these methods for periodic hard realtime tasks. Very limited work has been done on real-time system with mixed tasks which include periodic as well as aperiodic tasks [4,5].This is because periodic tasks are easier to schedule as meeting deadline is the only constraint whereas performance of the aperiodic tasks depends on how early it can finish its execution. The schedule should take care of responsiveness of the aperiodic tasks along with reduced dynamic energy consumption. This paper proposes an energy aware real-time scheduling algorithm -Energy Efficient Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (EEDVFS) for mixed task set. DVFS is applied on periodic and aperiodic tasks to reduce energy consumption without compromising on periodic task deadlines and aperiodic task responsiveness.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes related work. The proposed algorithm is discussed in Section 3. Section 4 and 5 details the experimental setup and results respectively. Finally, Section 6 concludes the work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Energy optimization through scheduling can be achieved by addressing platform dependent factors like preemptions and cache impacts or by addressing platform independent factors like supply voltage and clock frequency.

Conventional real-time schedulers [6] like EDF, RM and LLF are designed for periodic tasks to meet all task deadlines without bothering about energy consumption. Slack stealing is one of the widely used techniques for executing aperiodic tasks [7].Various other scheduling algorithms like Deferrable Server (DS) [8], Sporadic Server (SS), Total Bandwidth Server (TBS) [6], Constant Utilization Server (CUS) [9] etc were developed for mixed task set consisting of periodic and aperiodic tasks.

Many researchers have proposed static voltage and frequency scaling algorithms for periodic task set [2,10,11] and for mixed task set [4,5,12,13] to reduce energy consumption. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling of existing scheduling algorithms for periodic task system uses three types of dynamic slack estimation methods [2,3,4,5]:

(1) stretching to NTA (2) priority-based slack-stealing method and (3) utilization updating method. DVFS based online scheduling algorithms for periodic tasks were developed based on one of the above mentioned dynamic slack estimation methods [2,10,11,14,15]. They were implemented either on fixed priority or dynamic priority scheduling policy. Some of the existing DVFS algorithms for periodic task system were experimentally validated in [1].

Existing DVFS techniques for periodic task set can't be directly applied to mixed task set consisting of periodic and aperiodic tasks due to arbitrary temporal behavior of aperiodic tasks. There are another set of slack estimation methods. They are [5] M-lppsRM (Modified low power priority scheduling Rate Monotonic) [13], M-lppsRM-S and M-lppsRM-B [5] are based on fixed priority scheduling policy. First one is implemented using stretching to NTA with DS while other two uses SNRT and BSS respectively with DS and SS. Other few algorithms are based on dynamic scheduling policy with CBS or TBS. Slack estimation methods used by EDF based algorithms is shown in table I. In this paper, we have implemented utilization updating DVFS technique using DS where periodic task use available slack time and aperiodic tasks are executed at maximum frequency to get better responsiveness.

div.head: III. PROPOSED ALGORITHM
div.p: The proposed algorithm-EEDVFS -is a dynamic priority scheduling algorithm using DVFS technique. It schedules the mixed task system which includes both periodic and aperiodic tasks. EEDVFS follows EDF decisions at each decision point and uses utilization updating as DVFS technique.

The scheduler selects the next job from ready queue or aperiodic queue and assigns it to the processor. It also selects appropriate frequency and voltage for that job. Fig. 1 describes step-wise procedure of EEDVFS scheduler to select next job to run and calculate voltage and frequency of selected job respectively. Inputs and expected output along with the algorithm is described below. RET in fig. 1 is Remaining Execution Time.

div.head: A. Input:
div.p: Periodic task set T = {T 0 , .....,T n-1 } where n is the total number of periodic tasks in a task set. Each periodic task is represented as {R i , P i , C i , D i }. Each periodic task T i has k instances {J 0 , ..., J k-1 }in a hyper-period where k = hyperperiod/P i . Aperiodic task set A = {A 0 ,.....,A m-1 } where m is the total number aperiodic tasks in an aperiodic task set. Each aperiodic task is represented as {A i , C i }. Aperiodic server used is DS and is denoted as T ds = {P ds , C ds }. Let Ready Queue be RQ, Aperiodic Queue be AQ at current time t, E i be the actual execution time of Job i at maximum frequency f max . J <i,k> denote k th job of i th task in a task set. f scaled and v scaled are scaled frequency and scaled voltage respectively which is computed using utilization updating method.

div.head: B. Output:
div.p: Next job to run in CPU with clock frequency and supply voltage or ERROR if a periodic job is missing its deadline. U i is utilization of periodic job at time t, U ds is utilization of aperiodic job and UT is total utilization. T <i,j> denote j th job of i th task in a task set. If the period of the aperiodic server is smaller than the smallest period of the periodic task and if the deadline is same as period, then no periodic task which is arriving at time t will have priority higher than aperiodic server. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

In this paper, we have implemented EDF based DS with and without DVFS which schedules periodic and aperiodic tasks. Both the algorithms are implemented in C language. Various performance metrics such as response time, latency, preemption count, number of decision points and energy consumption are measured.

The algorithms are tested on synthetic benchmark programs. The benchmark programs are generated using random number generators. The number of periodic tasks in a task set varies from 2 to 20. The number of aperiodic tasks in a task set can be 2, 3 or 5. In case of DS with DVFS, for each periodic task, actual execution time is generated for the number of instances till its hyper period using random EEDVFS_scheduler:

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: We have compared EEDVFS and DS on performance metrics such as energy consumption and response time. Total utilization is fixed to 70% and number of aperiodic tasks are fixed to 2. Energy consumed by the two algorithms are computed for task sets where number of periodic tasks are ranging from 2 to 20. Fig. 2 shows normalized energy consumption by EEDVFS and DS. It shows 54.44% of energy saving by EEDVFS. Fig. 3 shows responsiveness of aperiodic task by both the algorithms. It is observed that there is no degradation in response time by the proposed algorithm. Existing non-DVFS algorithm DS is also implemented. EEDVFS is compared with DS. Extensive simulation is carried out on synthetic benchmark programs. The results showed that the proposed energy efficient algorithm saves 54.44% of energy as compared to non-DVS algorithm with no degradation in responsiveness of aperiodic tasks.
